## Model Limitations — What the Gurney Cylinder Assumption Ignores

The Gurney cylinder model is a deliberate simplification. Here is what it omits,
in plain terms:

**1 · The shell is not just a cylinder.**
A real artillery shell has three distinct zones: a pointed nose (ogive), a cylindrical
body, and a flat base. The Gurney *cylinder* formula models only the body. The nose
fragments spray forward at steep upward angles; the base fragments spray backward
and downward. Together these zones account for roughly 20–30 % of the steel mass
but produce none of the fragments in the single-cylinder model. Gold (2007) explicitly
accounts for the tail boom and fuze as separate mass contributors; the one-region
PAFRAG assumption treats the entire shell as a single cylinder, omitting both end
zones (Gold 2017, §2). Consequence: the single-zone (equatorial-belt) field, taken
alone, *underestimates* total fragment count and carries no forward- or rear-sector
hazard.

*Complemented by the four-zone field (§6), not replaced:* the four-zone
decomposition (§6.1) assigns ogive, cylinder, boattail, and base each their own
Mott distribution, Gurney velocity, and spray angle, adding the forward ogive
sector and the rearward base sector. The single-zone belt is **deliberately
retained** alongside it as the drawing-data-free, absolute-magnitude baseline —
the reference the four-zone lobe structure is measured against (three-variant
division of labor, §6). This is a coexisting pair, not an old-to-new
progression. Residual limitations of the zone model are listed in §12.

**2 · Fragments do not all fly in one horizontal plane.**
The cylindrical body does spray predominantly sideways (Figure 4 cross-section), but
even within the cylinder there is an elevation spread around horizontal caused by the
oblique angle at which the detonation wave meets the wall. Gold (2007, Figs. 3 and 9)
shows fragment velocity varying continuously with spray angle ψ; the elevation spread
is roughly ±15°–30°. The v 0.1.0–0.2.0 model put every fragment at exactly θ = 0°
(horizontal), missing fragments that fly over a prone target or clip a standing target
near the head or feet.

*Partially addressed in v 0.3.0:* each zone now sprays at its own elevation angle
(ogive ≈ 80°, boattail ≈ 95°, base ≈ 165°), so fragments are no longer constrained
to horizontal. Within-zone spread (±5°–10° around each zone's midpoint normal) is
still not modelled — see limitation #4.

**3 · One velocity for every fragment.**
Gurney gives a single initial speed V₀ for all fragments, regardless of mass, position
in the shell, or local explosive density. Gold (2007, Fig. 9) shows the measured
fragment velocity distribution spanning roughly ±10–15 % around the Gurney mean. The
Mott distribution already captures mass spread; combining it with a velocity
distribution would widen the lethality envelope at short range and narrow it at long
range. The Gurney constant itself (2 440 m/s for TNT) is a nominal tabulated value;
aging, temperature, and lot-to-lot density variation can shift it by a few percent,
which propagates linearly into V₀ and quadratically into fragment kinetic energy
(no collected source — general explosive engineering).

**4 · Single midpoint spray angle per zone (no elevation spread).**
Each zone is assigned one spray elevation angle (the surface normal at the arc midpoint).
Gold (2017, Fig. 9) shows that fragment velocity varies with polar angle within a zone,
producing an elevation spread of ±5°–10° around the midpoint. This spread is not
modelled; all fragments from a zone are treated as leaving at the same angle. The
effect is smoothed out when the hazard field is integrated over many azimuths, but
peak density near the zone boundary may be slightly overestimated.

**5 · Shell parameters are not sourced from a collected document.**
Wall thickness, projectile mass, and filler mass are taken from US Army TM 9-1901
(cited in code comments) but that manual is not collected in `doc-reference/`.
If these inputs are wrong, every output shifts — V₀ scales with M/C, and μ scales
as r_bu³.

- **The 75 mm M48 entry models the *fielded production round*** (TM-9-1904
  14.6 lb, official 1.47 lb TNT, M48-family fuze + M20/M20A1 booster). Tolch
  (1938) — the only fragmentation dataset this shell is validated against —
  fired 1938 T3 articles with M39 fuzes and an average 1.56 lb TNT fill, ~6 %
  heavier. Case metal agrees between the two to 0.4 %, but Gurney $V_0$ in
  Tolch comparisons runs ~3 % low for this reason
  ([`updates/75mm-fuze-case-mass-fix/derivation.md`](updates/75mm-fuze-case-mass-fix/derivation.md)
  §3).

**6 · Mott input uncertainties amplify super-linearly.**
The break-up radius r_bu is derived from the V/V₀ ≈ 3 expansion criterion, which
Gold (2017, §2) describes as "accepted as a rule of thumb for routine one-region
PAFRAG modeling" with only fair agreement to high-speed photography. Steel ductility
variation means harder steel fractures earlier (smaller r_bu, smaller fragments) and
softer steel fractures later; this carries ~10–20 % uncertainty in r_bu. Because
μ ∝ r_bu³ (Gold 2017, eq. 5), a 15 % error in r_bu produces a 50 % error in μ.
Similarly, γ and σ_F each carry ~25 % uncertainty — Mott (1947, §3) brackets
γ at 53–67 for steels ranging from 0.25%C to 0.45%C — and both enter μ as the 3/2
power (Gold 2017, eq. 5), giving roughly 35–40 % uncertainty in the fragment size
scale. The R₅₀ sensitivity sweep above captures the σ_F range but not the joint
uncertainty.

**7 · All fragments are tumbling irregular chunks.**
The drag model uses a single *population-average, orientation-averaged* pair
C_D = 1.28, C_shape = 2.089 (combined 2.674, §4) — one constant retardation
rate per fragment mass, with no orientation distribution. Felix et al. (2022,
§2.3) document that real fragments are 2–6× longer than they are wide, and note
that shape "has a significant effect on the air resistance restricting the
velocity of the fragment." Some of these elongated splinters fly with their long
axis aligned to the velocity vector (edge-on), producing C_D ≈ 0.2–0.4 and
reaching further than the model predicts. The fraction of aero-stable splinters
is not known from first principles; arena tests suggest it is a small minority
but they dominate the far-field hazard. The v0.9.0 anchor below corrects the
population average; it does not introduce the orientation spread, so this
limitation stands (and the *relative* excursion of an aero-stable splinter is
now measured against a 4.6× larger baseline retardation — not re-quantified
here).

*Provenance — resolved in v0.9.0, and still do not conflate two uses of Felix
et al. (2022).* The citation above sources only the **qualitative** point that
elongated, edge-on-flying splinters have lower drag (C_D ≈ 0.2–0.4); Felix et
al. give no baseline drag magnitude at all (their quantitative shape result is a
1:1.6–1.7 aspect ratio), and the Catovic et al. (2012) drag paper they cite is
not collected in `doc-reference/`. That distinction is what kept the former
constants (C_D = 0.65, C_shape = 0.90, combined 0.585) unsourced: 0.65 rested on
Cunniff (2014, §4; Driels K_d ≈ 0.66) and was disputed by Vigil (SAND92-0243,
1992, C_D = 1.0–1.71), while C_shape = 0.90 had no source at all. Both are now
**superseded and sourced** — C_D = 1.28 is DDESB TP-12's supersonic-plateau
value and C_shape is *derived*, not fitted, from the same source's measured
ballistic density $k = 2600$ kg/m³ via $C_\text{shape} =
(\rho_\text{steel}/k)^{2/3}$
([`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/derivation.md`](updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/derivation.md)
eq. 4, §2). The old 0.585 was not merely unsourced but *geometrically
impossible* (it implies a fragment 3.2× denser than steel presenting less area
than a sphere of equal mass, §3 there). This also settles the v0.8.0 mismatch
between `C_shape` and the Mott prism shape factor $\alpha$: the ordering
sphere 1.209 < cube 1.500 < the shape-closure prism's tumbling average 1.61 <
adopted 2.089 is the expected one for an irregular, non-convex-hull-filling
fragment measured by icosahedron gage, whereas 0.90 sat below even the sphere.

*What remains open* — carried from that update's own limitations
([`derivation.md`](updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/derivation.md) §7), not
re-opened here:

- **L1 — Tolch's absolute perforating count still over-predicts ~4–6×, and this
    is not attributed to drag.** Tolch (1938) is a *compound* test (drag × Mott
    spectrum × a fitted energy threshold × a perforate/not model), so its
    residual is not attributable to the retardation law; the Ordnance velocity
    anchor, which exercises retardation alone, is followed instead. Do not
    re-litigate this by re-fitting drag — the discriminating test is an
    independent (THOR-type) perforation model.
    **Addendum to L1, corrected — the "Mott stage exonerated" inference was
    void; the residual is partly in the population after all.** A scoping
    pass (`challenges/count-gap-1938/count-chain.md`) decomposed the 4–6×
    algebraically and originally concluded "the residual is in the
    perforating *fraction*, not the population" — that inference is
    **withdrawn**
    ([`count-gap-1938/rebaseline-verdict.md`](challenges/count-gap-1938/rebaseline-verdict.md)):
    a threshold-free test matching cumulative *mass fraction* instead of
    imposing a mass cut removes the fitted threshold, the drag chain, and the
    spray geometry from the comparison entirely, and the model still
    over-counts by 1.2–2.7×. The residual is **predominantly** in the
    perforating fraction (~2.1× of the ~3.9× at the fitted threshold), but
    ~1.2–2.7× of it is a genuine fragment-*spectrum* term that survives with
    the threshold removed — so the gross fragment population is partly the
    defect, not exonerated from it. ($N_0=3016$ for 75mm M48 — the currently
    shipped value after the M48 fuze/case-mass correction
    ($M_{case}=4980.0$ g, $V_0=864.4$ m/s, $\mu=0.826$ g; earlier revisions of
    this paragraph read 3597, then 3627 on the pre-fix case mass) — still falls
    *between* Tolch's own two totals: 5000 issued, **779** pit-recovered
    (corrected from a published 803 — see `rebaseline-verdict.md`); that
    bracketing argument survives the restatement even though the exoneration
    drawn from it does not.) The model's fitted $E_{thr}$ (1.9–3.6 J) still declares
    81–85% of fragments perforating where Tolch measures 14% (700/5000); at
    Tolch's own sourced hole-size bound (126 J) the fitted-threshold
    component of the residual drops to ~1.7–2.1×. Ranking is otherwise
    unchanged — C1 (the fitted threshold itself, the only unbounded term)
    needs a perforation model `src/arty/` does not have (THOR-type, or a
    sourced softwood ballistic limit); C2 (`mott_params` evaluates $x_0$ at
    the terminal Gurney $V_0$ rather than the case's actual break-up-radius
    velocity, 1.2–2×, right direction) cannot be fully separated from the
    genuine spectrum term without C1. Both remain deferred — a perforation
    model and a Mott-spectrum recalibration are future scope, not this
    pass's.
- **L2 — arrival-Mach < 0.7 velocities remain unclosed by any admissible drag
    law.** At the longest 75 mm/155 mm stations the *required* combined constant
    falls to 1.76–2.07 (implied C_D below the subsonic plateau of 1.08), and even
    a full Mach-dependent Fig-3 integration under-predicts velocity up to 2.4×.
    Free-fall terminal velocity is 20–23 m/s against 117–154 m/s observed, so
    gravity is not the explanation. These arrivals are already below the casualty
    threshold, so this sits outside the fidelity bar.
- **L3 — the drag anchor does not close `challenges/drag-gap-1944/`.** It cuts
    far-field lethal counts ~3× and narrows the *B(r)* over-prediction to
    ~1.9–5.3×, but the residual must be sought in the count chain, the spray/belt
    geometry, or the *B(r)* reduction itself — **not** in further drag increases:
    the geometric envelope leaves at most ~10 % of headroom above 2.674 before
    the fragment must be denser than a solid steel cube.

A Mach-dependent $C_D(M)$ — the fix the pre-v0.9.0 text called for, on the
grounds that the decay curve had the wrong *shape* rather than the wrong scale —
was implemented as a trajectory integration over the digitized TP-12 Fig-3 curve
and **rejected on evidence**: it scores no better than the corrected constant on
the same 1944 Ordnance data, which is the source's own recommendation
(`derivation.md` §5). The wrong-shape reading was an artefact of sweeping only
the 1.0–1.71 band (SAND92-0243's own parameter-range-list data floor/ceiling,
not its "1.2 and 1.7" prose sentence — see `drag-coefficient-calibration.md`),
which stops short of the geometrically admissible constant.

**8 · Lethality model assumes no protection and open ground.**
The ES-310 Pk|hit curve (FAS/Navy 1998) is calibrated for standing unprotected
infantry: the 4 kJ "heavy kill" anchor is explicitly described as the
armour-penetrating threshold, meaning the lower anchors (100 J, 1 kJ) apply to bare
flesh only. Three scenarios are unmodelled: (a) body armour reduces torso
vulnerability by a factor of roughly 3–5×; (b) a soldier in a foxhole or behind
cover has only their head and shoulders exposed, reducing presented area by ~80–90 %;
(c) ground ricochet can redirect fragments that would otherwise miss — particularly
relevant at shallow angles of fall. All three effects are bounded and could be added
as scalar multipliers on the presented area w.

**9 · Poisson statistics break down at high fragment density.**
p_kill = 1 − exp(−N_eff) is correct for a single target: if multiple lethal
fragments hit, the target is still dead once, and the formula saturates to 1.
The ES-310 multi-hit formula (FAS/Navy 1998) gives the same per-target result via
Pk = 1 − (1 − Pk|hit)^N_hits. For a *formation*, however, the model computes each
soldier's p_kill independently using the full fragment flux — it ignores depletion
(a fragment that kills soldier A is unavailable to kill soldier B). At close range
(≤ 50 m) with squad-density formations, this overestimates total expected kills.
The fix is a hypergeometric draw over the finite fragment count; it is not needed
for single-target or sparse-formation analysis.

**10 · The fragment distribution is continuous — there are no individual fragments.**
N_eff is computed by integrating the Mott PDF n(m) over mass, treating the fragment
cloud as a smooth density rather than a discrete set of projectiles. This gives the
ensemble-mean outcome over many rounds; a single detonation will produce a finite
count of fragments that scatter around that mean. For the bulk of sub-gram fragments
this is a good approximation — the count is large and the law of large numbers
applies. For the heavy tail (multi-gram fragments, counts in the tens to hundreds),
the discrete nature matters: a single large fragment that happens to land on a target
is a rare but high-consequence event that the mean integral undersells. Monte Carlo
simulation — drawing a finite sample from the Mott distribution and propagating each
fragment individually — would capture this variance. The threshold above which
discrete sampling is preferable to the continuous integral is not yet determined.

**11 · Lethality threshold: kill vs. wound semantics (from A7).**
The ES-310 Pk(KE) curve anchors lethality at 100 J (10% kill), 1 kJ (50% kill), and
4 kJ (90% kill), calibrated against pistol-calibre rounds on a uniformed soldier.
British WW2 research (1941) established that ~1 g splinters require only ~6.8 J to
produce an incapacitating wound in unprotected tissue — roughly 15× below the ES-310
10% floor. The two thresholds measure different outcomes:

| Source              | Outcome modelled                         | ~50% threshold (1 g fragment) |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| British 1941        | Wound (skin penetration, bare flesh)     | ~6.8 J                        |
| German Rohne        | Incapacitation (uniformed soldier)       | ~80 J                         |
| ES-310 (this model) | Kill (remove from combat)                | ~1 000 J                      |

Consequence: fragments below ~100 J are assigned Pk = 0. A 1 g fragment carries 100 J
only out to ~90 m slant range; the British data suggest it wounds to ~250 m. Since
the Mott distribution peak for a 105 mm shell is near 0.3 g (by count), the model's
lethality estimate is carried almost entirely by the multi-gram tail and will
understate area effect relative to WW2 casualty data if "wound" is the operational
criterion. See §9.2 for the Sturdivan tissue-penetration model as a future replacement.

**12 · Four-zone model assumptions (v 0.3.0).**

- **Tier-2 default CRH = 6.0** for shells without drawing-derived ogive arc
  geometry is an *engineering convention*, not sourced from any document
  in `doc-reference/`. CRH = 6 is representative of WW2 HE shells (M1 is
  6.02, M107 is 6.74); the resulting spray angle is in the [75°, 88°]
  band but the precise value carries ~ ±3° uncertainty.
- **Base-zone spray angle θ^b = 165°** is phenomenological. No primary
  source in `doc-reference/` resolves the rearward fragment cone angle of
  a thick base plate driven by axial detonation rarefaction. The value is
  consistent with the qualitative "strongly rearward but not exactly 180°
  due to finite base diameter" observation in NWC TP 7124 but is not
  literature-anchored.
- **Posture box-body dimensions** ($w_\perp, h, d$ for STANDING and PRONE,
  and the 0.85 m² standing frontal area they imply) are a NATO
  casualty-modelling **engineering convention**, not a value pending a
  citation. Both references once named as canonical for it *are* collected —
  [`wound-ballistics/cunniff-2014/`](../../doc-reference/wound-ballistics/cunniff-2014/cunniff-2014.md)
  and
  [`wound-ballistics/aep-55-vol3/`](../../doc-reference/wound-ballistics/aep-55-vol3/card.md) —
  and **neither carries a quotable man-silhouette presented area**. Cunniff's
  "presented area" is the *fragment's* projected area $A_p$ in the
  $A_d A_p/m_p$ penetration parameter, and its extraction states no
  tabulated standing/crouching/prone silhouette — checked against that
  extraction's own text, not against Cunniff's primary PDF (the extraction
  carries no card.md or retained source.pdf; see its provenance note), so
  treat this half of the pairing as secondhand. AEP-55 Vol. 3 is an armoured-vehicle
  IED test standard that assesses occupants with instrumented
  anthropomorphic test devices; a man-silhouette area is not a quantity its
  method uses, and a search of all 106 pages returns zero hits for any
  presented-area term (see the Vol. 3 card, which also flags the
  0.082 m² Annex E thorax-model area as a look-alike that must **not** be
  read as a silhouette). So collecting further references cannot discharge
  this caveat — it is a convention, and treating absolute posture-resolved
  hit counts as ±25 % engineering estimates is the standing disclosure, not
  an interim one.
- **$R_{50}$ recalibration pending.** The geometry-factor change from the
  width-based $s^{-1}$ form to the area-based $s^{-2}$ form in eq. (22')
  changes absolute hit counts: the new model is *smaller* by a factor of
  roughly $w_\perp h/(w \cdot s)$, i.e. of order $1.7/s$ (see
  target-area-profile derivation §4.3). The calibrated $R_{50}$ values
  must be re-anchored against TM 9-1901 lethal-area data once the new
  factor is in place. Until then, **absolute** lethal radii from the
  four-zone field are unreliable; *relative* zone contributions and
  lobed structure are valid.
- **Base equivalent-column $C^b_\text{eff}$** convention (derivation
  §3.3) is a geometric approximation, not literature-sourced.
- **Single-zone legacy path retains a `sinΘ` term for notational parity,
  with an error bound that grows with the spray half-angle δ.** The
  Family-A geometry factor in the single-zone legacy path
  (`_expected_kills_3d_point`/`_expected_kills_3d_vec`) keeps the field
  point's own polar-angle `sinΘ` term to match the pre-3D width-based
  formula (target-area-profile derivation §4.1.2), rather than the pure
  inverse-square form. Its deviation is `1/sin(90°−δ)−1`: 3.5 % at the
  app's default δ = 15°, rising to ≈15.5 % at the app's maximum
  δ = 30° (`spray_half_angle` slider). This is a proportional scaling of
  off-belt-centre cells only — no qualitative reversal of field shape or
  $R_{50}$ — and applies **only** to the single-zone ("legacy") path; the
  four-zone Family-A path (`_four_zone_familyA_eval`) divides by the
  fixed per-zone spray angle `sin(theta_z)` instead and does not carry
  this error at all.
- **AoF-resolved validation data** is not present in any of BRL 126,
  NWC TP 7124, or SAND92-0243. The four-zone lobed structure is a
  qualitative prediction (forward density > rearward at AoF < 90°) that
  cannot yet be checked against empirical fragment-density-vs-azimuth
  data.
- **The single-zone − four-zone difference map is a co-located zone
  attribution, up to a bounded off-belt normalization residual.** The
  sensitivity app's "Four-zone − Single-zone" diff (§6) is *grid-exact*
  (both fields share the same grid, so no interpolation error enters). The
  single-zone belt path (`_expected_kills_3d_vec` /
  `_expected_kills_3d_point`) and the four-zone Family-A path
  (`_four_zone_familyA_eval`) now share the **same forward shell-axis
  convention** $\hat{e}=(+\cos\alpha,0,-\sin\alpha)$ (shell-axis-fix,
  `updates/legacy-field-shell-axis-fix/derivation.md`), so both
  down-range lobes sit on the same side of the burst and the diff is a
  co-located per-zone residual rather than the mirror-opposite sum of two
  lobes it used to be. The only remaining mismatch is the off-belt-centre
  `sinΘ` normalization difference noted above (single-zone keeps the point's
  own `sinΘ`; four-zone divides by the fixed per-zone `sin(theta_z)`),
  bounded by `1/sin(90°−δ)−1` (≤ 15.5 % at δ = 30°) and identically zero on
  the equatorial belt centre. The map is therefore a valid directional and
  per-zone attribution; only the few-percent off-belt magnitude residual is
  not an exact lethality difference.
- **Hard-cutoff spray belts create unphysical dead zones between zone
  boundaries.** Each zone's contribution to a ground point is gated by a
  ±15° (``delta_deg``) rect-function band around the zone's nominal spray
  angle. Ground positions falling between belts — the ≈ 0°–65° nose shadow
  and the ≈ 110°–150° gap between boattail and base — receive zero fragment
  density, appearing as white regions in the hazard map. In reality the
  spray distribution is smooth and continuous (Gold 2017, Fig. 9). The
  fix is to replace the hard acceptance test with a smooth angular weight
  (e.g., Gaussian in polar angle), which also correctly handles overlap
  between adjacent zones.
- **Residual bias from the false-safe-zone fixes (Family B v 0.5.1, Family A
  v 0.6.0).** Both of the two kill-probability pathways (§*Two
  kill-probability pathways*) originally scored the near-burst ring $P_k=0$
  at steep AoF, since each sampled the fragment field on the $z=0$ ground
  plane only; both are now fixed (Change Log 0.5.1/0.6.0; derivations at
  `updates/target-height-intercept/derivation.md` and
  `updates/familyA-false-safe-zone/derivation.md`; Family B's fix is also
  derived and illustrated above in §*Point Kill Probability*). Each fix
  leaves a different residual bias: Family B scores frontal projection only,
  leaving prone exposure under steep arrival **conservative-low**; Family A
  scores the full presented area whenever any part of the column is lit,
  over-counting a head-only grazing strike at the full silhouette —
  **conservative-high**, confined to the thin inner ring. In both, the true
  innermost dead zone under the burst ($r\lesssim(h_b-h)/\tan\delta$)
  correctly remains $P_k\approx0$.
- **Base-zone (and light-shell boattail-zone) thin-plate excursion post
  shape-closure.** The base zone's (and, on lighter shells, the boattail
  zone's) fragment shape closure now implies `t_bu > x̄` — the fragment
  thickness exceeds its own breadth, 1.2×–7.1× depending on shell/zone, past
  the thin-plate regime this closure assumes (registry whole-shell worst
  case: 1.14×, `mott-fragment-shape-closure/derivation.md` §5 item 5). This
  inflates `μ^base` 17×–38× vs. the pre-fix cube formula (vs. 3.5×–9.4× for
  ogive/cylinder) and can move the rendered rear-lobe `P(kill)`/lethal-density
  magnitude by a factor of ~2–3×. Treat the base-zone (and boattail-zone,
  lighter shells) lobe magnitude as lower-confidence than the ogive/cylinder
  lobes; not corrected here per the same reasoning as the 60 mm mortar
  limitation above.

**13 · The baseline steel grade's *composition* is an inference, not a source
(v 0.7.0).**
What is sourced about the default `WW2 US HE Shell` entry is its **name only**:
"Steel WD-X1335, spec 57-107", from the 105 mm M1 bill of material
(`doc-reference/ww2-shells/ordnance-105mm-m1-1940/card.md` p. 16). Spec 57-107
is not digitised, so the composition **0.33–0.38 % C** quoted for that grade is
read off the AISI 1335 data sheet on the *unconfirmed* hypothesis
**WD-X1335 ≈ AISI 1335** — an inference from grade-name similarity, not a second
sourced fact (the AISI card carries no WD-series linkage, and SAE 1040 at
0.40 % C is an equally plausible analog). This is asymmetric with the
`US WW2 WDSS1` entry, whose 0.14–0.20 % C *is* a direct transcription of
*Ammunition Series 6* Table 6-1. Consequence: the *direction* of the carbon
ranking between the two catalogued grades is safe — every candidate analog for
WD-X1335 sits well above WDSS-1's band — but its *magnitude*, and every "% C"
figure quoted for the baseline, inherit the inference. Since the 2026-08-08
re-anchor the shipped parameter **does** depend on it: $\gamma' = 54.5$ is a
local-linear interpolation of Mott's recomputed $\gamma$ column *at* the
inferred 0.355 % C midpoint (§9.1), where the superseded $\gamma = 65$ was
merely bracket-anchored. The composition *band* itself is cheap (0.33–0.38 % C
moves $\gamma'$ only 54.1–54.9); the exposure is the grade identity, if
WD-X1335 is not an AISI 1335 analog at all. Closing this needs spec 57-107 or an
equivalent WD-series chemistry table. Three related residues from the same
derivation (`updates/wdss1-steel-grade/derivation.md`, §7 as amended by §9):

- **The modelled grade contrast is now rule-consistent, and modest (A5).**
  Both catalogued entries sit on **one rule and one column** since the
  re-anchor: $\gamma'$ = 54.5 (baseline, 0.355 % C) and 47 (WDSS-1, 0.17 % C)
  are both local-linear interpolations of the same recomputed Mott column. The
  earlier "largest defensible contrast, −38.5 % on $N_0$, upper bound" reading
  is **withdrawn**: at M1 geometry the contrast is $\mu$ +16.0 %, $N_0$
  −13.8 %, $N(>0.5\,\text{g})$ −10.5 %. Direction and grade ordering are
  unchanged; the effect size is ~14 % on $N_0$, not ~39 % — a second-order
  material sensitivity, not a headline.
- **Mechanical properties are unsourced for both grades (A6).** Table 6-1 is
  chemistry-only: no yield strength, no heat treatment. $\sigma_F = 800$ MPa is
  a shared reporting convention, not a per-grade measurement — legitimate only
  because the Mott closure (eq. 4) sees the pair solely through the ratio
  $\sigma_F/\gamma$, so the grade difference is carried entirely by $\gamma$.
  An earlier working band of 0.18–0.28 % C for WDSS-1, from a secondary
  attribution that Table 6-1 contradicts, is flagged for review and used
  nowhere.
- **$R_{50}$ is the wrong readout for grade choice (C8).** The −13.8 % move in
  $N_0$ shifts $R_{50}$ by only −1.2 % (45.42 → 44.89 m): fewer, heavier
  fragments each retain lethal KE further out, and the two effects very nearly
  cancel. Post-shape-closure $R_{50}$ rises **weakly and monotonically** with
  $\gamma'$ over the whole plausible range (43.5 m at $\gamma' = 35$ → 45.8 m at
  $\gamma' = 65$), so the softer WDSS-1 grade *shortens* $R_{50}$ slightly
  rather than lengthening it — the earlier "+2.5 %, broad maximum at
  $\gamma = 47$" reading was computed before the shape closure and the drag
  re-anchor and is withdrawn. Either way the conclusion stands: read grade
  effects on fragment *count and mass distribution*, not on lethal radius.

**14 · Check 5b's lethality-criterion half is an open discrepancy, not a
pass (v 0.9.0).**
[Check 5b](_validation.qmd) (3.5 g fragment at 61 m, British WW2
weight-of-fire, 50% lethality) splits into two independent halves because the
source's lethality criterion and the model's ES-310 `Pk|hit` curve are not the
same scale (limitation 11). The **kinematic** half — retained KE against the
source's own 58 ft-lb (78.6 J) marginal-lethality energy — passes to a
factor-of-2 band under the v0.9.0 drag anchor
(`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/derivation.md` §4 — the anchor half of
that update, which remains live). The **criterion**
half does not: ES-310 reads 0% against the source's 50%, an 11.6× stricter
scale (ES-310 half-kill at 1 kJ vs. the source's 78.6 J), and is reported, not
asserted, rather than tuned away. The pre-v0.9.0 model appeared to pass this
check, but by compensating error: the superseded drag constant (combined
0.585) gave a retardation length 4.5× too long, holding the fragment at 834 J
— 10.6× the historical criterion — which happened to land near ES-310's 1 kJ
half-kill point (`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/checks/check5b-drag-spotcheck.py`).
Closing this needs either a documented ES-310-to-source criterion mapping or
an independent source for the 50%-lethality energy threshold itself; neither
exists in `doc-reference/` today. No shipped parameter depends on this check
passing — it is a spot-check, not a calibration target.

**Addendum to 14 — Family A's agreement with the 1944 card is the same
confound, not independent evidence.** Family A's own B(r)-vs-card comparison
(`challenges/drag-gap-1944/b-vs-range-familyA.md`) numerically passes the
factor-of-2 band at all 33 tabulated points, but only because it multiplies
Family B's ~2–5× fragment-count over-prediction against the card's own 58
ft-lb threshold by Family A's ES-310 curve being ~10× stricter than that same
threshold — two offsetting, threshold-confounded errors, verified to cancel
algebraically at every row (review in `challenges/drag-gap-1944/review.md`).
It must not be read as validating the Family-A kernel, or as closing the
lethality-criterion split above; the fix is the same one this item already
names — a threshold-matched Family A variant, not yet built.

**Second addendum to 14 — the 1944 *B(r)* comparison carries no angular
information, in either family.** The card's $B$ column is
$N_\text{eff}/(4\pi r^2)$ *by construction*: an isotropic reduction of a total
count over a sphere. Whatever agreement a model reaches against it — Family B's
re-baselined factor-of-2 pass
([`challenges/drag-gap-1944/b-vs-range-rebaseline.md`](challenges/drag-gap-1944/b-vs-range-rebaseline.md)),
or Family A's confounded one above — tests only the **direction-averaged**
effective-fragment density and its range decay. A model with the correct total
count and a completely wrong side-spray belt would score identically on every
row of every table in that document. **This agreement must not be cited as
external support for the model's side-spray belt or its four-zone angular
structure**; nothing in `doc-reference/` currently validates the angular
distribution, and the zone geometry rests on the sourcing recorded in
limitation 12. Criterion-match ruling:
[`challenges/source-data-audit/review-criterion-match.md`](challenges/source-data-audit/review-criterion-match.md)
§1b′.

**15 · Fragment drag is speed-dependent. The model does not represent that —
it uses one constant $C_D$ at every speed (v 0.9.0).**
Real fragment drag varies with Mach number, and the source the model is
anchored to shows exactly how much: DoD-1975 Figure 3 gives $C_D$ = 1.08 at
$M = 0$, a transonic peak of 1.40 near $M = 1.5$, and a supersonic plateau of
1.28 ([`tables/figure-3-drag-coefficient.csv`](../../doc-reference/fragmentation/dod-1975-fragment-debris-hazards/tables/figure-3-drag-coefficient.csv)) —
a ~30% swing, of which the model represents none. `DragParams.C_D` is fixed at
the supersonic plateau value 1.28, so $\lambda$ is a constant per fragment mass
and $v(s) = V_0 e^{-\lambda s}$ holds in closed form. Fragments therefore decay
too slowly through the transonic peak they actually cross, and too quickly once
subsonic.

*This is a deliberate simplification, and the reason is architectural, not
evidential.* A Mach-dependent $C_D(M)$ integrated along each trajectory is
**genuinely more accurate** on the corrected 1944 Ordnance velocity data: given
both laws the same single scale freedom, it reduces RMS log-velocity error by
~20–25% on both the casualties and perforation columns. In the lethal-relevant
band ($M > 0.7$, casualties column) the Mach law scores 5.3% against the
constant's 7.1%. Both land inside the aspect's stated ±10% arrival-velocity
fidelity bar, so the ~1.8-percentage-point difference is immaterial at the
target — while adopting it would replace a closed-form $\lambda$ with a
per-fragment ODE march at every call site, including the field kernel's single
broadcast exponential over the whole mass × standoff grid. Rejected as
**immaterial at the stated fidelity target, not as unsupported by the data.**

*Provenance — and a correction to what this notebook previously published.*
Through v0.9.0 the change log and governing-equations section stated that a
Mach-dependent $C_D$ "does not beat the constant" on this data. **That claim was
false and is withdrawn.** It rested on a digitized Figure-3 curve that
under-stated $C_D$ by up to 0.082 across Mach 1.0–2.2 — in the direction that
weakened the rejected candidate — and on a 25-point velocity set that was ~44%
wrong-column, and it scored a *fitted* constant against an *unfitted* curve.
The decision survives the correction; the stated reason did not. Full ruling:
[`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/rebaseline-verdict.md`](updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/rebaseline-verdict.md)
(C11, C12), independently verified in
[`challenges/source-data-audit/review-void-rulings.md`](challenges/source-data-audit/review-void-rulings.md).
That update is now closed and half-retired — see its
[`README.md`](updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/README.md) before citing
anything in it.

*What would re-open this.* A fidelity target tighter than ±10% on arrival
velocity, or any use of the model in the sub-$M$-0.7 regime where limitation
7's carried **L2** already records that no admissible constant closes the
velocities. Note
also that $V_0$ for the Ordnance comparison is itself unverified, and a 10%
$V_0$ error is comparable to the entire residual — so the 1.8-point margin
quoted here is a measured difference between two laws, not a bound on either
law's absolute accuracy.

*And what the comparison data actually are.* The 1944 Ordnance $(r, m, v)$
triples that both laws are scored against — the ones read by
[`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/checks/mach-law-rebaseline.py`](updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/checks/mach-law-rebaseline.py) —
are **the source's own period variable-drag ballistic calculation, not
arrival-velocity measurements**. They are internally consistent with a computed
decay law rather than with instrumented arrivals: the retardation grouping
$\lambda\,m^{1/3}$, which is constant along a column for any single fixed-$C_D$
law, drifts 1.4–1.7× down the casualties columns while staying flat to ~5 % on
the perforation columns. Every velocity comparison in this item is therefore
**model-against-period-model agreement**, not model-against-measurement, and
residuals below the 1944 law's own (undocumented) accuracy are not
interpretable — including the ~1.8-percentage-point Mach-vs-constant margin
above. It bounds what the check can license, not its arithmetic: the ±10 %
fidelity bar is stated against a 1944 calculation, and no measured
fragment-arrival-velocity set for these shells exists in `doc-reference/` to
replace it. Criterion-match ruling:
[`challenges/source-data-audit/review-criterion-match.md`](challenges/source-data-audit/review-criterion-match.md)
§2d.
